Required Readings

[M] David R. Mayhew. 2004. Congress: The Electoral Connection. 2nd ed. Yale University Press. ISBN: â9780300105872.Â 

[K] Keith Krehbiel. 1998. Pivotal Politics. University of Chicago Press. ISBN: â9780226452722.Â 

[R] David W. Rohde. 1991. Parties and Leaders in the Postreform House of Representatives. University of Chicago Press. ISBN: â9780226724072.Â

Week 1

No readings assigned.

Week 2: Theories of legislative behavior

Donald R. Matthews. 1959. âThe folkways of the United States Senate.â American Political Science Review, vol. 53, pp. 1064â1089.

Richard F. Fenno. 1962. âThe House Appropriations Committee as a political system.â American Political Science Review, vol. 56, pp. 310â324.

[M] Introduction, Chap. 1, and pp. 141â158. [Preview with Google Books]

Kenneth A. Shepsle and Barry R. Weingast. 1994. âPositive theories of congressional institutions.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 19, pp. 149â179.

[K] Chaps. 1â2. [Preview with Google Books]

Week 3: Congressional representation

Richard F. Fenno. 1977. âU.S. House members and their constituencies: An exploration.â American Political Science Review, vol. 71, pp. 883â917. (The book-length treatment is Home Style, which you should be familiar with eventually.)

Justin Grimmer. 2013. âAppropriators not position takers: The distorting effects of electoral incentives on congressional representation.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 57, pp. 624â642.

David E. Broockman. 2016. âApproaches to studying policy representation.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 41, pp. 181â215.

Week 4: Representation of race, gender, religion, and class

David T. Canon. 1999. Race, Redistricting and Representation, chap. 4. University of Chicago Press. ISBN: â9780226092713.Â 

Michele L. Swers. 1998. âAre women more likely to vote for women’s issue bills than their male colleagues?â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 23, pp. 435â448.

Nicholas Carnes. 2012. âDoes the numerical underrepresentation of the working class in Congress matter?â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 37, pp. 5â34.

Nicole Asmussen Mathew. 2018. âEvangelizing Congress: The emergence of evangelical Republicans and party polarization in Congress.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 43, pp. 409â455.

Week 5: Congressional elections

Edward R. Tufte. 1975. âDeterminants of the outcomes of midterm congressional elections.â American Political Science Review, vol. 69, pp. 812â826.

Gary Jacobson. 1978. âThe effects of campaign spending on congressional elections.â American Political Science Review, vol. 72, pp. 469â491.

Donald P. Green and Jonathan S. Krasno. 1988. âSalvation for the spendthrift incumbent: Reestimating the effects of campaign spending in House elections.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 32, pp. 884â907.

Robert S. Erikson and Thomas R. Palfrey. 2000. âEquilibria in campaign spending games: Theory and data.â American Political Science Review, vol. 94, pp. 595â609.

Jowei Chen and Jonathan Rodden. 2013. âUnintentional gerrymandering: Political geography and electoral bias in legislatures.â Quarterly Journal of Political Science, vol. 8, pp. 239â269.

Nicholas O. Stephanopoulos and Eric M. McGhee. 2015. âPartisan gerrymandering and the efficiency gap.â University of Chicago Law Review, vol. 82, pp. 831â900.

Week 6: Congressional candidates, careers, and the incumbency advantage

Robert S. Erikson. 1971. âThe advantage of incumbency in congressional elections.â Polity, vol. 3, pp. 395â405.

David R. Mayhew. 1974. âCongressional elections: The case of the vanishing marginals.â Polity, vol. 6, pp. 295â317.

Thomas E. Mann and Raymond E. Wolfinger. 1980. âCandidates and parties in congressional elections.â American Political Science Review, vol. 74, pp. 617â632.

Bruce E. Cain, John A. Ferejohn, and Morris P. Fiorina. 1984. âThe constituency service basis of the personal vote for US representatives and British members of Parliament.â American Political Science Review vol. 78, pp. 110â125. (NB: This is essentially the same argument as the Cain, Ferejohn, and Fiorina book, The Personal Vote, in the âadditional readings.â)

Gary C. Jacobson. 1989. âStrategic politicians and the dynamics of U.S. House elections, 1946â1986.â American Political Science Review, vol. 83, pp. 773â793. (NB: This is essentially the same argument as the Jacobson and Kernell book, Strategy and Choice, in âadditional readings.â)

Stephen Ansolabehere, James M. Snyder, Jr., and Charles Stewart III. 2000. âOld voters, new voters, and the personal vote: Using redistricting to measure the incumbency advantage.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 44, pp. 17â34.

âââ. 2001. âCandidate positioning in U.S. House elections.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 45, pp. 136â59.

Jamie Carson, Eric Engstrom, and Jason Roberts. 2007. âCandidate quality, the personal vote, and the incumbency advantage in Congress.â American Political Science Review, vol. 101, pp. 289â301.

Gary C. Jacobson. 2015. âIts Nothing Personal: The decline of the incumbency advantage in U.S. House elections.â Journal of Politics, vol. 77, pp. 861â73.

Week 7: Committees

Richard F. Fenno. 1973. Congressmen in Committees, Introduction, chaps. 1â2. Little, Brown.

Kenneth A. Shepsle. 1979. âInstitutional arrangements and equilibrium in multidimensional voting models.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 23, pp. 27â59.

Kenneth A. Shepsle and Barry R. Weingast. 1987. âThe institutional foundations of committee power.â American Political Science Review, vol. 81, pp. 85â104.

Thomas W. Gilligan and Keith Krehbiel. 1990. âOrganization of informative committees by a rational legislature.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 34, pp. 531â564. {NB: The core of this articleâs argument is further developed â along with a comprehensive critique of then-extant theories of legislative organization â in Krehbielâs book, Information and legislative organization, in the âadditional readingsâ section.)

Forrest Maltzman and Steven S. Smith. 1994. âPrincipals, goals, dimensionality, and congressional committees.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 19, pp. 457â476.

James M. Curry. 2019. âKnowledge, expertise, and committee power in the contemporary Congress.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 44, pp. 203â237.

Week 8: Parties and leadership I

[R] Chaps. 1â3, skim the rest. [Preview with Google Books]

Joseph Cooper and David W. Brady. 1981. âInstitutional context and leadership style: The House from Cannon to Rayburn.â American Political Science Review, vol. 75, pp. 411â425.

David W. Brady. 1985. âA reevaluation of realignments in American politics: Evidence from the House of Representatives.â American Political Science Review, vol. 79, pp. 28â49.

Jason M. Roberts and Steven S. Smith. 2003. âProcedural contexts, party strategy, and conditional party voting in the U.S. House of Representatives, 1971â2000.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 47, pp. 305â317.

David R. Rohde. 2013. âReflections on the practice of theorizing: Conditional party government in the twenty-first century.â Journal of Politics, vol. 75, pp. 849â864.

Sarah Binder. 2018. âDodging the rules in Trumpâs Republican Congress.â Journal of Politics, vol. 80, pp. 1454â1463.

Week 9: Parties and leadership II

[C] Chaps. 1 and 2. [Preview with Google Books]

Keith Krehbiel. 1993. âWhereâs the party?â British Journal of Political Science, vol. 23, pp. 235â266.

Stephen Ansolabehere, James M. Snyder, and Charles Stewart III. 2001. âThe effects of party and preferences on congressional roll-call voting.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 26, pp. 533â572.

Frances E. Lee. 2009. Beyond Ideology. Chaps. 1, 7, and 8. University of Chicago Press. ISBN: â9780226470764. [Preview with Google Books]

Andrew J. Clarke. 2020. âParty sub-brands and American party factions.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 64, pp. 452â470.

Week 10: Decision-making

Keith T. Poole and Howard Rosenthal. 1991. âPatterns of congressional voting.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 35, pp. 228â278.

Joshua Clinton, Simon Jackman, and Douglas Rivers. 2004. âThe statistical analysis of roll call data.â American Political Science Review, vol. 98, pp. 355â370.

Keith T. Poole, and Howard Rosenthal. 2001. âD-NOMINATE after 10 years: A comparative update to Congress: A political-economic history of roll-call voting.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 26, pp. 5â29.

Jason M. Roberts, Steven S. Smith, and Stephen R. Haptonstahl. 2015. âThe dimensionality of congressional voting reconsidered.â American Politics Research, vol. 44, pp. 794â815.

Week 11: Policymaking and interbranch relations

Mathew D. McCubbins and Thomas Schwartz. 1984. âCongressional oversight overlooked: Police patrols versus fire alarms.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 28, pp. 165â179.

Terry M. Moe. 1987. âAn assessment of the positive theory of congressional dominance.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 28, pp. 475â520.

Nolan M. McCarty and Keith T. Poole. 1995. âVeto power and legislation: An empirical analysis of executive and legislative bargaining from 1961 to 1986.â Journal of Law, Economics, & Organization, vol. 11, pp. 282â312.

Jeffrey A. Segal. 1997. âSeparation-of-powers games in the positive theory of Congress and courts.â American Political Science Review, vol. 91, pp. 28â44.

Charles M. Cameron and Nolan McCarty. 2004. âModels of vetoes and veto bargaining.â Annual Review of Political Science, vol. 7, pp. 409â435. (NB: This article contains much of the core of Cameronâs book, Veto Bargaining, which is listed among the additional readings.)

Hans J. G. Hassell and Samuel Kernell. 2015. âVeto rhetoric and legislative riders.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 60, pp. 845â859.

Nolan M. McCarty, Keith T. Poole, and Howard Rosenthal. 2016. Polarized America: The Dance of Ideology and Unequal Riches, chap. 2. 2nd ed. MIT Press. ISBN: â9780262528627. [Buy at MIT Press.] [Preview with Google Books]

Nolan McCarty, Keith T. Poole, and Howard Rosenthal. 2009. âDoes gerrymandering cause polarization?â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 53, pp. 666â680.

Thomas L. Brunell and Justin Buchler. 2009. âIdeological representation and competitive congressional elections.â Electoral Studies, vol. 28, pp. 448â457.

Joseph Bafumi and Michael C. Herron. 2010. âLeapfrog representation and extremism: A study of American voters and their members in Congress.â American Political Science Review, vol. 104, pp. 519â542.

Marc Trussler. 2020. âGet information or get in formation: The effects of high-information environments on legislative elections.â British Journal of Political Science, vol. 51, pp. 1529â1549.

Week 13: History and development of Congress

Jeffery A. Jenkins and Charles Stewart III. 2018. âThe deinstitutionalization (?) Of the House of Representatives: Reflections on Nelson Polsbyâs ‘The Institutionalization of the House of Representatives’ at Fifty.â Studies in American Political Development, vol. 32, pp. 166â187.

Jonathan N. Katz and Brian R. Sala. 1996. âCareerism, committee assignments, and the electoral connection.â American Political Science Review, vol. 90, pp. 21â33.

Sarah Binder. 1996. âThe partisan basis of procedural choice: Allocating parliamentary rights in the House, 1789â1990.â American Political Science Review, vol. 90, pp. 8 â 20. (NB: This is a boiled-down version of her book, Minority rights, majority rule, in the âadditional readingsâ section for this week.)

Eric Schickler. 2000. âInstitutional change in the House of Representatives, 1867â1998.â American Political Science Association, vol. 94, pp. 269â288.

Sarah Binder. 2006. âParties and institutional choice revisited.â Legislative Studies Quarterly, vol. 31, pp. 513â532.

Eric Schickler and Gregory Wawro. 2004. âWhereâs the pivot? Obstruction and lawmaking in the pre-cloture Senate.â American Journal of Political Science, vol. 48, pp. 758â774.
